name: Tapinarof

angle.text: Tapinarof is a prescription cream used to clear visible plaques in psoriasis and eczema. It is labelled for those conditions with phase 3 support; its use for seborrheic dermatitis has not been backed by trials found.

summary: A prescription AhR-agonist cream for psoriasis and eczema with phase 3 support; seborrheic dermatitis use is not yet backed by trials found.
currentQuick:
Tapinarof (Vtama) is a steroid-free cream approved in the US for plaque psoriasis and atopic dermatitis.
Phase 3 trials support psoriasis; it is described as under study for seborrheic dermatitis, with no trial found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: It activates the aryl hydrocarbon receptor in skin cells, which lab studies link to reduced inflammation and improved barrier proteins. The label says its exact mechanism is unknown.
Risks and caveats: Label-listed reactions in psoriasis include folliculitis, nasopharyngitis, contact dermatitis and headache. Pregnancy data in humans are insufficient. Prescription only.
deepLead:
Tapinarof (brand name Vtama) is a 1% topical cream and an aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) agonist. The US FDA label lists it for plaque psoriasis in adults and atopic dermatitis in adults and children aged 2 and older. Its mechanism in these conditions is described on the label as unknown, although laboratory work shows it binds and activates AhR in skin cells.
Two phase 3 trials in plaque psoriasis were published in 2021, and a phase 2b trial in atopic dermatitis reported efficacy in adolescents and adults. Seborrheic dermatitis is described as under study, but no trial for it appears in the sources reviewed.

name: Roflumilast cream

angle.text: Roflumilast cream and foam are prescription products approved for psoriasis, eczema and scalp or facial seborrheic dermatitis, used to clear visible redness and flaking. Phase 3 data support its psoriasis and eczema use.

summary: A prescription PDE-4 inhibitor cream and foam approved for psoriasis, eczema and scalp or facial seborrheic dermatitis, with phase 3 data for psoriasis and eczema.
note: Prescription-only; not studied for vitiligo in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Roflumilast cream (Zoryve) is a steroid-free topical approved in the US for plaque psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis (foam) and atopic dermatitis.
Phase 3 randomized trials support the psoriasis and eczema uses; off-label talk about vitiligo has no trials behind it in the sources found.
How it works: It selectively inhibits phosphodiesterase-4, an enzyme involved in inflammatory signaling in skin.
Risks and caveats: Prescription only. Topical adverse events are reported in trial publications and the label; oral roflumilast tablets list diarrhea, nausea, headache and insomnia.
deepLead:
Roflumilast cream (brand name Zoryve, developed by Arcutis) is a topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitor. The US FDA approved the 0.3% cream for plaque psoriasis in July 2022, a 0.3% foam for seborrheic dermatitis in December 2023, and a 0.15% cream for atopic dermatitis in July 2024. Seborrheic dermatitis and psoriasis are visible skin conditions, which is the basis of its appearance relevance.
Phase 3 trials have tested it in plaque psoriasis and atopic dermatitis. Other uses such as vitiligo are not supported by trials in the sources reviewed.

name: Sofpironium

chain: Dry shirts, no visible sweat marks
angle.text: Sofpironium is a prescription underarm gel for excessive sweating, used to keep clothing dry and free of visible sweat marks. It is trial-backed for hyperhidrosis and approved in Japan as Ecclock; it is a medical treatment rather than a cosmetic.

summary: Prescription topical anticholinergic gel for underarm sweating; trial-backed for hyperhidrosis, not a cosmetic.
note: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention) are listed on the label.
currentQuick:
Sofpironium is a prescription gel applied to the underarms to reduce excessive sweating (primary axillary hyperhidrosis). It was first approved in Japan in 2020 and is sold in the US as Sofdra.
It relates to appearance only indirectly, as a grooming-adjacent medical treatment; no looksmaxxing community discussion is documented.
How it works: It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors on sweat glands where it is applied, reducing the signal that triggers sweating.[4][6]
Risks and caveats: Label-listed adverse reactions include dry mouth, blurred vision, dilated pupils, skin irritation and urinary retention; the label also warns about lack of sweating in hot conditions.[6]
deepLead:
Sofpironium bromide is a topical anticholinergic gel developed by Bodor Laboratories and licensed to Brickell Biotech for primary axillary hyperhidrosis (excessive underarm sweating). It is designed to reduce sweating by blocking M3 muscarinic receptors in eccrine glands at the application site. It received its first approval in Japan in September 2020 under the brand name Ecclock.
In the United States the product is sold as Sofdra, and its label lists the indication as primary axillary hyperhidrosis in adults and pediatric patients aged 9 years and older. Its relevance to appearance is indirect: underarm sweat is a grooming and clothing concern, and the gel is a prescription medicine for a recognised medical condition rather than a cosmetic product.
Randomized trials have compared the gel with vehicle (an inactive gel). Anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision and urinary retention are listed on the US label.

name: Dexpanthenol

angle.text: Dexpanthenol is a barrier-supporting, soothing ingredient in skincare used for hydrated, calmer-looking skin. It has been studied mainly for wound healing and skin irritation rather than appearance outcomes.

summary: Vitamin B5 derivative in soothing, barrier-support skincare; studied mainly for wound healing and irritation.
note: Evidence is mostly for wound healing and irritated skin, not cosmetic appearance outcomes.
currentQuick:
Dexpanthenol is a form of vitamin B5 found in many moisturizers and ointments, usually marketed for soothing dry or irritated skin.
Research has looked mainly at wound healing and radiation-related skin reactions, with small trials.
How it works: It is converted to pantothenic acid, a part of coenzyme A that supports normal epithelial function, and is thought to act as a humectant on skin.[1]
Risks and caveats: Topical use is described as well tolerated in the reviews listed; this entry does not cover injected B-vitamin products.
deepLead:
Dexpanthenol (also panthenol, provitamin B5) is the stable alcohol analog of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). Pantothenic acid is a component of coenzyme A and is described as essential to normal epithelial function; topical dexpanthenol is used on skin because it penetrates well and reaches high local concentrations. It appears in barrier-supporting and soothing skincare products, often as a humectant at concentrations of a few percent.
Research on topical dexpanthenol has centred on wound healing, skin irritation and radiation-related skin reactions rather than on cosmetic outcomes. A 70th-anniversary review of its topical use and a 2020 review on wound healing summarize this literature.

name: Calendula extract

angle.text: Calendula extract appears in soothing skincare for calmer-looking, less irritated skin. Studies have looked at wound healing, and no appearance-specific trials have been found.

summary: Marigold flower extract used in soothing skincare; studied for wound healing, with no appearance-specific trials found.
note: Research is mainly on wound healing and animal or lab models.
currentQuick:
Calendula extract comes from pot marigold flowers and is used in topical products for soothing skin.
Research has examined wound healing and oral mucositis, plus animal and lab work on inflammation; appearance-specific trials were not found.
How it works: Laboratory studies report anti-inflammatory activity of flower extracts; the mechanism in human skin is not established in the sources reviewed.[4]
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not describe significant adverse effects of topical use; safety data are limited to the small studies cited.
deepLead:
Calendula extract is a preparation from the flowers of Calendula officinalis, used in topical skincare and traditional wound-care products. Laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory properties for flower extracts, and human and animal studies have examined it mainly for wound healing.
A 2019 systematic review of calendula extract as a single treatment for wound healing covered 14 studies, 7 animal experiments and 7 clinical trials. No published trial listed here has tested it for cosmetic appearance goals such as acne or skin aging.

name: Ciclopirox shampoo

angle.text: Ciclopirox shampoo is a prescription antifungal wash used to clear scalp flaking and redness from seborrheic dermatitis. Several vehicle-controlled trials support that use; none have examined hair growth.

summary: A prescription antifungal shampoo with several vehicle-controlled trials for scalp seborrheic dermatitis and none for hair growth.
note: Prescription-only in the US; trials address dandruff-type scalp inflammation, not hair loss.
currentQuick:
Ciclopirox shampoo is a medicated shampoo with an antifungal that is used for seborrheic dermatitis, the inflamed, flaky scalp condition related to dandruff. It is prescription-only in the US.
Randomized trials have tested the 1% shampoo against vehicle for scalp seborrheic dermatitis and as an adjunct in childhood tinea capitis. Hair-loss communities sometimes mention it alongside ketoconazole, but no trial found tested it for hair growth.
How it works: Ciclopirox is a hydroxypyridone antifungal with a mechanism that differs from the azoles and is not fully understood; it is active against Malassezia yeasts and is described as having anti-inflammatory properties.
Risks and caveats: Systemic absorption from topical use is reported to be low. It is a prescription medicine in the US and Canada; local irritation is the usual concern with medicated shampoos.
deepLead:
Ciclopirox shampoo is a medicated shampoo containing the synthetic hydroxypyridone antifungal ciclopirox, used mainly to treat seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, a common inflammatory condition that causes flaking, redness and itching and overlaps with ordinary dandruff. Ciclopirox is a broad-spectrum antifungal with reported anti-inflammatory properties and is active against Malassezia yeasts, which are implicated in seborrheic dermatitis.
In appearance and hair-loss communities, ciclopirox shampoo is sometimes mentioned as an alternative or companion to ketoconazole shampoo for scalp flaking and, more speculatively, for scalp health in people with hair loss. Published trials have examined it for seborrheic dermatitis and, as an adjunct, for tinea capitis (scalp ringworm) in children; no published trial found in the sources examined tested it as a hair-growth treatment.
In the United States, ciclopirox is a prescription-only medicine, according to Wikipedia.

name: Climbazole

angle.text: Climbazole is an antifungal found in anti-dandruff shampoos and conditioners, used to reduce visible flaking. It belongs to the same class as ketoconazole; research in the sources is mostly environmental, with little clinical data cited.

summary: An azole antifungal found in anti-dandruff shampoos; research in the sources is mostly environmental, with little clinical data to cite.
note: Little published clinical trial data; regulators have flagged environmental concerns.
currentQuick:
Climbazole is an azole antifungal added to over-the-counter dandruff shampoos and conditioners, sometimes alongside zinc pyrithione. It targets Malassezia yeast linked to dandruff.
Most published studies on it deal with its presence in wastewater and wildlife rather than with scalp outcomes. A clinical study from 2001 is cited by Wikipedia, but no trial results were available for this article.
How it works: Like ketoconazole, it is described as inhibiting the fungal enzyme CYP51, which blocks ergosterol production in fungal membranes.
Risks and caveats: Local irritation such as redness and itching is reported. Grokipedia describes cosmetic-use limits in the EU and a 2024 ECHA flag for possible endocrine-disrupting properties; it is also reported as toxic to aquatic life.
deepLead:
Climbazole is a synthetic imidazole antifungal used as an active ingredient in over-the-counter anti-dandruff shampoos, lotions and conditioners, and sometimes as a preservative. It belongs to the same azole class as ketoconazole, clotrimazole and miconazole and is active against Malassezia yeasts thought to contribute to dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis.
Most published research found on climbazole concerns its detection and fate in the environment rather than clinical effect on the scalp: studies have measured it in wastewater, rivers and fish, and one has examined its ecotoxicity. Wikipedia cites a 2001 clinical study of a climbazole dandruff shampoo for seborrheic scalp eczema, but no trial details were available for this article.

name: Coal tar shampoo

angle.text: Coal tar shampoo is an old-school over-the-counter wash used to clear dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis flakes. Trials support its effect on scalp flaking; it stains and smells strongly, which limits acceptance.

summary: An old-school tar-based dandruff and psoriasis shampoo with trial support for scalp flaking and long-running carcinogenicity debates.
note: Coal tars are IARC Group 1 carcinogens; the EU forbids coal tar in cosmetics per Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
Coal tar shampoo contains tar from coal processing and is sold over the counter for dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis. It is known for its odor and staining.
Older studies reported it effective for these conditions, while a double-blind trial found a non-tar shampoo as effective for dandruff. It is not used for appearance beyond scalp flaking.
How it works: Coal tar is a complex mixture, and Wikipedia does not describe how it works; it is traditionally called keratolytic and anti-inflammatory.
Risks and caveats: Irritation, folliculitis, phototoxicity and contact dermatitis are reported. Coal tars are IARC Group 1 carcinogens, and Wikipedia reports the EU forbade coal tar in cosmetics in 2009.
deepLead:
Coal tar shampoo is a medicated shampoo containing coal tar, a viscous dark by-product of coke and coal-gas production, sold over the counter for dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and scalp psoriasis. Wikipedia notes that patient acceptance is limited because tar products can stain, smell strongly and be messy.
Controlled studies from 1980 to 2000 reported it effective in psoriasis, dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, while a double-blind trial found a non-tar shampoo was as effective as a 0.5% coal tar shampoo for dandruff. Coal tars are classified by the IARC as Group 1 carcinogens, and a mid-1990s correspondence in The Lancet debated the carcinogenic potential of coal tar shampoo and measured skin uptake of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons after hair washing.

name: Glycerin

angle.text: Glycerin is a common moisturizer, cleanser and shaving ingredient used to keep skin hydrated and soft-looking. Its long use is well documented; cosmetic trials of glycerin itself were not found in the sources reviewed.

summary: The ubiquitous humectant in moisturizers and cleansers, with long use but no cosmetic trials in the sources reviewed.
note: Evidence for skin effects here is descriptive; diethylene glycol contamination has been a historical safety issue.
currentQuick:
Glycerin is a thick, sweet, water-attracting liquid that appears in most moisturizers, soaps and many hair and shaving products. It is also used as a laxative, drug excipient and food additive.
The sources reviewed describe its role as a humectant but contain no cosmetic trials; the registered trials found study other uses such as suppositories.
How it works: It is hygroscopic, so it attracts and holds water, which is why it is described as a humectant that softens skin.
Risks and caveats: Oral toxicity is described as very low, but large amounts can affect children, and past diethylene glycol contamination caused deaths, leading to FDA batch-testing advice in 2007.
deepLead:
Glycerin (glycerol) is a colorless, odorless, sweet-tasting, viscous sugar alcohol that is miscible with water and hygroscopic, meaning it draws in moisture. It is one of the most common ingredients in skin care, hair care, soaps, shaving products and personal lubricants, where it functions as a humectant and gives a smooth feel.
Beyond cosmetics it is widely used in medicine and food: as a laxative in suppositories, as an excipient in tablets and syrups, and as the food additive E422. The sources reviewed for this article contain no randomized trial of glycerin as a cosmetic moisturizer, so its skin effects here rest on encyclopedic descriptions and use history rather than on trial data.

name: Lanolin

chain: Smoother, less chapped lips and skin
angle.text: Lanolin is an emollient wax used in lip balms and moisturizers to soften dry, chapped skin and lips. It resembles lipids in human skin; trials have focused mainly on sore nipples rather than facial appearance.

summary: A wool-derived emollient wax in lip balms and moisturizers, with allergy history and trials aimed mainly at sore nipples.
note: A recognized contact allergen for some people; purified grades are sold as low-allergen.
currentQuick:
Lanolin is a waxy substance from sheep wool that is refined into an emollient for moisturizers, lip balms, baby care and nipple creams.
It is described as long-lasting at holding moisture, but registered trials focus on breastfeeding nipple care and none were found for cosmetic purposes.
How it works: Its sterol and wax esters resemble skin lipids; it forms an occlusive layer and can take up water, which is why it is described as an emollient.
Risks and caveats: It is a relatively common contact allergen, though Wikipedia says its sensitizing potential was historically overstated. Purified, low-pesticide grades are standardized in the US and European pharmacopoeias.
deepLead:
Lanolin is a yellow, waxy substance secreted by the sebaceous glands of wool-bearing animals, mainly sheep, and recovered from wool washing; it is often called wool fat or wool wax although it is mainly sterol and wax esters rather than a true fat. Purified lanolin is a widely used emollient in skin care, lip balms, baby products and nipple creams, and it resembles lipids of human skin.
Lanolin is also a relatively common contact allergen, and Wikipedia describes the question of how sensitizing it really is as historically contested. Registered trials have compared lanolin with other topicals for sore nipples in breastfeeding women; Wikipedia states that evidence for a soothing effect is limited.

name: Dimethicone

angle.text: Dimethicone is used in primers, moisturizers and hair serums to leave a smooth, silky film that visibly softens the look of fine lines and pores and adds shine to hair. The smoothing is visible on application; trials cover medical skin-protectant uses rather than long-term appearance outcomes.

summary: A silicone oil used as a skin protectant and hair-smoothing ingredient; trials cover medical uses, not appearance outcomes.
note: Cosmetic safety panels rate it safe as used; liquid silicone injection is a separate, documented source of granulomas.
currentQuick:
Dimethicone is a silicone oil found in many moisturizers, primers, shampoos and conditioners. It gives a smooth, slippery feel and forms a water-repellent film on skin and hair.
Published human trials involve medical uses such as dermatitis and head lice; none were found testing it for improving appearance in healthy people.
How it works: It is a long-chain silicone polymer that is hydrophobic and leaves a thin protective layer on the surface of skin or hair, which accounts for its conditioning and smoothing effect.
Risks and caveats: The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded it is safe as used in cosmetics. Silicone granulomas reported in the literature arise from injected liquid silicone, not topical use. It is not biodegradable but is removed in wastewater treatment.
deepLead:
Dimethicone, also known as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) or dimethylpolysiloxane, is a silicone polymer and a type of silicone oil. It ranges from a pourable liquid to a rubbery semi-solid depending on chain length, and it is hydrophobic and optically clear.
In skin and hair products it is widely used as a skin-protectant and conditioning ingredient, listed in moisturizing lotions and sometimes present at concentrations up to about 15 percent, and in shampoos and conditioners to add slip and shine. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel has concluded that dimethicone and related polymers are safe as used in cosmetic formulations.
Published human studies of dimethicone concern medical uses such as incontinence-associated dermatitis and head lice rather than appearance outcomes. Consumers mainly encounter it as an ingredient in moisturizers and hair products, and product labels list it as a skin protectant.

name: Shea butter

angle.text: Shea butter is used as a rich moisturizer for dry skin, lips and hair ends, so skin looks softer and less flaky. It is promoted on the basis of traditional use and lab composition data; trials of shea butter alone for appearance are not found.

summary: A plant fat from African shea nuts used as an emollient; supported mainly by tradition and lab data, with no solo-ingredient appearance trials.
note: Refined grades may retain far less of the vitamin and phenolic content than unrefined butter.
currentQuick:
Shea butter is a creamy fat from the nuts of the African shea tree. It is used as a moisturizer, in hair products, in soaps and, in some regions, as a cooking fat.
Traditional use for dry skin and burns is well documented, and lab studies show anti-inflammatory compounds in it, but no trial found tests it alone for appearance.
How it works: It acts as an emollient, softening and coating the skin with fatty acids (mainly oleic and stearic). Lab work has examined triterpenes in the unsaponifiable fraction for anti-inflammatory activity.
Risks and caveats: Safety assessments cited by Grokipedia describe low toxicity for skin and oral use. Highly refined grades are reported to contain much less of the vitamin and phenolic content than raw butter.
deepLead:
Shea butter is a fat extracted from the nuts of the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows wild across the dry savanna belt of West and Central Africa. It is mainly a triglyceride fat rich in oleic and stearic acids, ivory in colour when unrefined.
It is used in cooking in parts of Africa, as a cocoa-butter substitute in confectionery, and in cosmetics as an emollient and skin conditioner, including in moisturizers, lotions, soaps and hair products. Traditional use for dry skin, burns and rashes is documented in ethnomedical accounts.
Evidence for specific cosmetic claims is limited: laboratory studies have examined its anti-inflammatory triterpenes, and small trials have tested shea-containing products, but no trial found tests shea butter alone for appearance outcomes.

name: Sodium PCA

angle.text: Sodium PCA is a humectant in moisturizers and toners, used to keep skin hydrated so it looks plumper and less dry. It occurs naturally in skin's moisturizing factor; safety is reviewed, but trials of the ingredient alone for appearance were not found.

summary: A skin-derived humectant salt used in moisturizers; safety is reviewed, but no appearance trials of the ingredient alone were found.
currentQuick:
Sodium PCA is a humectant found in many moisturizers, toners and hair products. It is the sodium salt of a compound the skin makes naturally as part of its moisture-retaining system.
It is rarely studied on its own, so evidence is mostly its safety review and its role in skin biology.
How it works: As a humectant it binds water. Pyroglutamic acid is a component of the skin's natural moisturizing factor, which is the basis for its use in dry-skin products.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia describes it as low in toxicity and not a skin irritant. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel has reassessed PCA and its salts for cosmetic use.
deepLead:
Sodium PCA is the sodium salt of pyroglutamic acid (2-pyrrolidone-5-carboxylic acid, also called sodium pyroglutamate or sodium pidolate). It is used in cosmetics as a humectant, an ingredient that attracts and holds water, in dry-skin and hair products.
Pyroglutamic acid is a natural component of the skin's natural moisturizing factor (NMF). The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel reassessed PCA and its salts, which it describes as functioning in cosmetics as skin-conditioning humectants.
Very little clinical research on sodium PCA itself was found; it appears mostly as one ingredient within formulations.

name: Sodium lactate

angle.text: Sodium lactate appears in moisturizers and cleansers as a humectant and pH adjuster, used to help skin hold water and feel softer. It is the salt of lactic acid, a familiar exfoliating acid, though its own appearance effects are less documented than its medical roles.

summary: A lactic acid salt used as a humectant and pH adjuster in personal care; its medical role is better documented than any appearance effect.
note: Intravenous sodium lactate is a medical product and can provoke panic attacks in people with panic disorder.
currentQuick:
Sodium lactate is a mild salt of lactic acid used in shampoos, liquid soaps and some moisturizers to hold water and balance pH. It is also a food preservative and part of hospital fluids such as Ringer's lactate.
No trials were found testing it for appearance.
How it works: As a humectant it attracts and holds water in a formulation, and as a salt of a weak acid it helps buffer pH.
Risks and caveats: In topical and food use it is generally regarded as low-risk by the sources reviewed. Intravenous use is medical, is contraindicated in lactic acidosis, and can induce panic attacks in people with panic disorder.
deepLead:
Sodium lactate is the sodium salt of lactic acid (formula C3H5NaO3), a white powder or colourless liquid with a mild saline taste. It is made by fermenting a sugar source such as corn or beets and neutralising the resulting lactic acid.
It is used as a food additive (E325) acting as preservative, acidity regulator and bulking agent, in shampoos and liquid soaps as a humectant, and in medicine as a component of Ringer's lactate solution. It does not contain milk protein.
Its relevance to appearance is as a minor moisturizing and pH-regulating ingredient in personal-care products; no trials were found testing it for appearance.

name: Trehalose

angle.text: Trehalose is added to some moisturizers and serums as a water-binding, protective sugar, and is discussed in anti-aging circles for its link to autophagy. Autophagy findings come from lab and animal research; appearance trials on skin are not found.

summary: A protective sugar used in food, eye drops and some skincare; interest is in autophagy research, not proven appearance benefits.
note: Autophagy findings come largely from cell and animal models; human trials are small.
currentQuick:
Trehalose is a sugar that many organisms use to survive drying and stress. People encounter it in foods, dry-eye drops and some moisturizers.
Research focuses on neurodegenerative disease and autophagy; no studies were found testing it for appearance.
How it works: It stabilises proteins and membranes during dehydration. In mammalian cells it has been reported to trigger autophagy, partly through the TFEB pathway, though the mechanism is debated.
Risks and caveats: It is broken down to glucose by trehalase and is generally treated as safe in foods. Trehalase deficiency is uncommon, and a link to C. difficile outbreaks was disputed by a 2019 study.
deepLead:
Trehalose is a non-reducing disaccharide made of two glucose units joined by an alpha,alpha-1,1 glycosidic bond. It occurs in bacteria, yeast, fungi, insects, invertebrates and plants but cannot be synthesised by vertebrates.
Commercially it is used in food as a mildly sweet stabiliser (about 45 percent as sweet as sucrose), in biopharmaceutical formulations, and in eye drops for dry eye. Cosmetic uses as a moisturizing and protective ingredient are reported, but the encyclopedic sources reviewed do not cover them in detail.
Research interest in trehalose centres on its induction of autophagy in neurodegeneration models; small human trials are registered, but no study found tests it for appearance.

name: Polyglutamic acid

chain: Polymer binds large amounts of water
angle.text: Polyglutamic acid is promoted in serums and essences as a humectant said to hold more water than hyaluronic acid, giving a plump, dewy look. Its established clinical use is as a drug carrier; appearance claims rest mainly on lab comparisons and brand testing.

summary: A bacterial-fermentation humectant polymer marketed in skincare; real clinical use is as a drug carrier, not for appearance.
note: Superior-to-hyaluronic-acid claims come from AI-generated or marketing sources, not from cited trials.
currentQuick:
Polyglutamic acid is a long chain of glutamic acid produced by Bacillus bacteria, also found in natto. Skincare brands use it as a water-holding ingredient.
Human trials involve cancer-drug conjugates rather than skin; none were found testing it for appearance.
How it works: The polymer is water-soluble and carries many negative charges, which lets it bind water and metals. In medicine it is attached to drugs such as paclitaxel to change how they are delivered.
Risks and caveats: Gamma-PGA is described as biodegradable and non-immunogenic. Wikipedia notes its medical use is largely pre-clinical, and safety data for topical cosmetic use were not found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Polyglutamic acid (PGA) is a polymer of the amino acid glutamic acid, existing as gamma-PGA (linked through the side-chain carboxyl) and alpha-PGA (linked through the alpha-carboxyl). Both forms are water-soluble and negatively charged.
Gamma-PGA is produced by Bacillus species through fermentation and is a major constituent of the Japanese food natto. It is listed as a cosmeceutical ingredient, and is promoted in skincare as a humectant; Grokipedia claims it holds more water than hyaluronic acid, a statement from an AI-generated source that is not backed by a cited trial here.
The best-documented human trials involve alpha-PGA as a carrier in the chemotherapy conjugate paclitaxel poliglumex. No trials found test PGA for skin appearance.

name: Propanediol

angle.text: Propanediol is a base ingredient in serums and moisturizers, used to hydrate, improve texture and help other actives dissolve and spread. It is chosen as a plant-derived alternative to propylene glycol; its role is supporting formulations rather than a studied appearance treatment.

summary: A glycol humectant and solvent that sits in the base of many skin products; it carries other actives rather than doing anything dramatic itself.
note: Allergic contact dermatitis reported in a small share of people.
currentQuick:
Propanediol is a family of small two-hydroxyl molecules. The 1,2- form (propylene glycol) and the 1,3- form are both used in cosmetics to attract water, dissolve other ingredients and help them spread.
It is a supporting ingredient, not a treatment. No human trials have tested it for skin appearance on its own.
How it works: As a humectant it binds water, and as a solvent and penetration enhancer it helps other ingredients dissolve and move into the upper skin layers, according to encyclopedic descriptions.
Risks and caveats: Toxicity is described as low, but contact allergy is reported in an estimated 0.8 to 3.5 percent of people depending on concentration, and propylene glycol was the American Contact Dermatitis Society's 2018 Allergen of the Year.
deepLead:
Propanediol is the name for a small group of organic compounds with the formula C3H8O2 in which two hydroxyl groups sit on a three-carbon chain. Two isomers matter commercially: 1,2-propanediol, better known as propylene glycol, and 1,3-propanediol, which is often made by fermentation and sold in cosmetics as a plant-derived alternative.
In skin care both isomers appear as solvents, carriers and humectants, meaning ingredients that attract and hold water and help dissolve other actives. They are rarely the focus of a product; they are listed on labels as part of the base of serums, moisturisers and makeup.
No published human trial has tested propanediol as a standalone appearance treatment. Its safety profile is described by encyclopedic sources as low in toxicity, with allergic contact dermatitis reported in a small share of people; the American Contact Dermatitis Society named propylene glycol its 2018 Allergen of the Year.

name: Ectoin

angle.text: Ectoin is used in soothing and barrier-support skincare, promoted to reduce redness and protect against UV and pollution stress for calmer, more even-looking skin. Lab data on UV stress exist; trials on appearance in healthy skin are not found.

summary: A bacteria-derived 'extremolyte' used in barrier and soothing skincare; lab data on UV stress exist, but appearance trials in healthy skin do not.
note: Human skin-hydration trial registered in atopic dermatitis; no results published in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Ectoin is a small molecule that salt-loving bacteria make to survive harsh conditions. Skincare brands use it in moisturisers and sun-care products for hydration, soothing and UV-stress protection.
Support comes mostly from lab studies in cells; a hydration and barrier trial in eczema is registered, and other ectoin products have been tested for airway, nasal and eye conditions.
How it works: It is described as a compatible solute that organises water around proteins and membranes and stabilises them; the 2004 cell study reported it limited several UVA-induced damage signals.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed describe it as well tolerated in nasal-spray use and report no specific skin safety concerns; formal safety data for cosmetic use are limited in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Ectoin (also spelled ectoine) is a small, water-soluble amino acid derivative produced by many bacteria that live in salty or otherwise stressful environments. It acts as a 'compatible solute', protecting cells from osmotic stress, and has been commercialised as a cosmetic and medical-device ingredient for skin soothing, hydration and UV-related protection.
In laboratory work, a 2004 study in cultured skin cells reported that ectoin reduced several markers of UVA-induced cell damage. A registered human trial has examined a 7 percent ectoin dermatitis cream for skin hydration and barrier function in atopic dermatitis, and other ectoin products have been studied for airway, nasal and eye conditions.
Ectoin is discussed mainly as a barrier-calming ingredient in skincare. No published trial has tested it for improving facial appearance in healthy people.

name: Beta-glucan

angle.text: Oat and yeast beta-glucan is used in creams and serums for soothing and hydration, so skin looks calmer and less dry. It is well studied as dietary fibre and an immune trigger; use as a topical appearance treatment is largely untested.

summary: An oat or yeast polysaccharide sold for soothing hydration; well studied as an immune-system trigger and dietary fibre, untested as a topical appearance treatment.
note: Skincare claims are not backed by trials in the sources reviewed; the research base is oral and immunological.
currentQuick:
Beta-glucans are sugar polymers from oats, barley, yeast and fungi. In skincare they appear in soothing and hydrating products, especially oat and yeast forms.
Most of the research concerns other roles: dietary fibre that lowers LDL cholesterol, and an immune-activating molecule recognised by dectin-1. Topical appearance trials are not found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Immune cells recognise beta-glucans through dectin-1 and related receptors. Cosmetic descriptions also cite water-binding and film-forming texture properties.
Risks and caveats: Oral forms are widely eaten as fibre. Sources reviewed list no specific topical safety signals, but also provide no topical safety trials.
deepLead:
Beta-glucans are a family of polysaccharides built from beta-linked glucose units, found in the cell walls of cereals such as oats and barley, yeasts, fungi, algae and some bacteria. Their structure, solubility and biological behaviour vary by source.
In skincare, oat and yeast beta-glucans are marketed as soothing, hydrating ingredients. Outside cosmetics, oat beta-glucan is best known as a soluble fibre for which the US FDA approved a heart-disease risk claim in 1997 relating to LDL cholesterol.
Laboratory immunology has established that beta-glucans are recognised by the immune receptor dectin-1 on macrophages. No clinical trial in the sources reviewed has tested topical beta-glucan for appearance outcomes.

name: Allantoin

angle.text: Allantoin is a common drugstore additive in moisturizers, lip balms and after-shave products, used to soften rough skin and calm irritation. It also appears in scar and wound combination products; allantoin tested on its own for appearance is rare.

summary: A classic soothing and moisturising additive in drugstore skincare; used in scar and wound combination products, rarely tested on its own.
note: Clinical studies are mostly on multi-ingredient products.
currentQuick:
Allantoin is a gentle, widely used skincare ingredient found in moisturisers, scar gels, lip products and sun care. Brands position it as soothing and hydrating.
Studies exist for scar and wound products that contain it, but they combine it with other ingredients, so its own effect is not isolated.
How it works: Cosmetic sources describe it as a humectant that attracts water and as having mild anti-inflammatory and antioxidant action. Humans do not make it enzymatically.
Risks and caveats: Described by Wikipedia as safe and non-toxic in cosmetic use, with a rat oral LD50 above 5,000 mg per kg.
deepLead:
Allantoin (5-ureidohydantoin) is a nitrogen-containing compound produced when uric acid is oxidised. Most mammals make it enzymatically; humans do not, and form only small amounts through reactions with reactive oxygen species. It is also found in plants such as comfrey, and cosmetic-grade allantoin is generally synthetic and described as chemically equivalent to the natural form.
It is a long-standing ingredient in over-the-counter skincare, toothpaste, shampoo, lipstick, sun-care and anti-acne products, where it is marketed for moisturising, soothing and skin-smoothing effects.
Clinical research on allantoin is mostly on combination products, particularly scar and wound formulations, so its individual contribution is hard to isolate. No trial in the sources reviewed tests allantoin alone for facial appearance.
